what.text: Minoxidil is a vasodilator: it widens small arteries. Taken by mouth it lowers blood pressure. A side effect, extra body hair, was seen in about 80% of people taking the tablets.

It comes in two approved forms in the US. A solution or foam put on the scalp is sold over the counter for hair regrowth on the top of the head. Tablets are prescription-only and approved only for severe high blood pressure.

src.label: Men's Rogaine Extra Strength label, DailyMed

what.text: Taking minoxidil by mouth for hair loss is off-label.

The sprays and strips that combine minoxidil with finasteride are compounded and are not FDA approved; no FDA-approved product combines minoxidil with finasteride. Oral minoxidil is not approved for hair loss.

research.text: Topical minoxidil has randomized trials behind its approval. Oral minoxidil for hair loss is off-label: one randomized trial, small open-label studies and a large retrospective safety review.

research.title: 5% vs 2% topical minoxidil (Olsen et al.)

facts.v: 393 men aged 18 to 49 with male pattern hair loss: 157 on 5%, 158 on 2%, 78 on placebo
scalp hair counts in a target area, patient and investigator ratings

research.found: 5% beat 2% and placebo on hair counts and ratings. Itching and local irritation were more common with 5%. No systemic effects were seen.

src.label: Olsen et al., J Am Acad Dermatol

research.title: Oral vs topical minoxidil (Penha et al.)

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial at one clinic
90 men aged 18 to 55 with male pattern hair loss; 68 finished
oral minoxidil 5 mg daily with a placebo solution, or topical 5% twice daily with a placebo tablet
terminal hair density on the front and crown, total density, photos

research.found: Oral minoxidil was not superior to topical on hair density. Photo review favored oral on the crown only. On oral minoxidil, 49% had extra body hair and 14% had headache.

research.title: Oral minoxidil in 30 men (Panchaprateep and Lueangarun)

facts.v: open-label, single arm. No control group, no placebo.
30 men aged 24 to 59 with male pattern hair loss
hair counts, hair diameter, photos, questionnaire, exams and lab tests

research.found: Total hair count rose by a mean of 35.1 hairs/cm² at week 24. Extra body hair occurred in 93% and ankle swelling in 10%. No serious heart events were seen.

research.title: Low-dose oral minoxidil safety, 1,404 patients (Vañó-Galván et al.)

facts.v: retrospective chart review at several centers. No control group.
1,404 patients (943 women, 461 men), mean age 43, any type of hair loss

research.found: Extra body hair in 15.1%. Lightheadedness 1.7%, fluid retention 1.3%, fast heartbeat 0.9%, headache 0.4%, swelling around the eyes 0.3%. 1.7% stopped for side effects. No life-threatening events were recorded.

research.text: No trial has tested compounded products that combine minoxidil with finasteride or other drugs.

In dogs, minipigs and rats, minoxidil caused heart lesions, including scarring in the heart muscle and bleeding in the heart wall. Some were produced by topical minoxidil absorbed into the blood. The label says their meaning for humans is not clear.

us.text: Topical minoxidil (Rogaine) was approved in 1988 and is sold over the counter today. Oral minoxidil (Loniten, 1979) is approved only for severe high blood pressure. Using it for hair loss is off-label.

items.text: NDA 018154, approved October 18, 1979. The brand is discontinued; FDA found it was not withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons. Generic tablets are prescription-only.
only high blood pressure that causes symptoms or organ damage and is not controlled by a diuretic plus two other blood pressure drugs.

the tablet label says: "Use of minoxidil tablets, in any formulation, to promote hair growth is not an approved indication." It adds that home-made or pharmacy-made topical forms should be treated as having the full range of the tablet's warnings.

us.text: Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

side.text: Oral minoxidil has a boxed warning: it can cause fluid around the heart and worsen chest pain. Topical minoxidil mostly causes scalp itching and irritation, but the label warns about heart symptoms and unwanted facial hair.

items.text: minoxidil "may produce serious adverse effects. It can cause pericardial effusion, occasionally progressing to tamponade, and angina pectoris may be exacerbated." The label reserves it for blood pressure that does not respond to a diuretic and two other drugs, given under close supervision, usually with a beta-blocker and a diuretic.

items.lead: Tablets, other effects on the label:
items.text: salt and water retention (temporary swelling in 7%), fluid around the heart in about 3% of patients not on dialysis, faster heart rate, extra body hair in about 80%, ECG changes in about 60%, rashes including rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and rare low platelet or white cell counts.

items.lead: Low-dose oral use for hair loss (off-label):
items.text: in the studies above, extra body hair was the most common effect (15% to 93%). Others were lightheadedness, fluid retention, fast heartbeat, headache and ankle or eye swelling.

items.text: the Rogaine label says to stop and ask a doctor for chest pain, rapid heartbeat, faintness or dizziness, sudden weight gain, swollen hands or feet, scalp irritation or unwanted facial hair. Ask a doctor first with heart disease. Hair color or texture may change. In the 48-week trial, itching and irritation were more common with 5% than 2%.

The UK status comes from EMA's lists of nationally authorised products (UK licence numbers); MHRA's own product records could not be read, and the UK sale category was not confirmed.
Canada's Loniten product monograph could not be downloaded, so its Canadian indication and Rogaine's non-prescription status were not confirmed from the monograph.
The oral minoxidil list from EMA dates from 2016; current EU authorisations of oral minoxidil were not confirmed.
surprises: The oral minoxidil label states that using it "in any formulation, to promote hair growth is not an approved indication," and that pharmacy-made topical forms should be treated as sharing the tablet's full warnings, which runs against common claims that compounded minoxidil sprays are low-risk.

The only randomized trial found here comparing oral and topical minoxidil (90 men, 24 weeks) found oral 5 mg was not superior to topical 5% on hair density, despite common claims that oral is stronger.
